vignette:
He is 21, European, married, and out of work, though the word "unemployed" feels too flat for the way he describes his days now. Before the trauma, he had been looking for steady work and spending a lot of time at home with his wife, imagining what it would be like to settle into something predictable. He talks about wanting an ordinary life. What changed was not something that happened to him directly, but something that happened to someone he loves, and the way that event split his life into before and after.

He describes the day of the trauma in careful pieces, as if each detail has to be placed in order so it can be contained. His wife was injured suddenly in an accident, and when he first heard, he thought it had to be a mistake. He remembers the immediate surge of disbelief, then the frantic drive, the waiting, the harsh overhead lights, and the way his mind kept trying to leap ahead to the worst possible outcome and then back again to denial. He says he kept calling her name before he could even see her, as though his voice could reach her through the chaos. When he finally saw her, he felt useless and terrified, standing there with no ability to fix anything. That helplessness remains one of the most painful parts of the memory for him. He says that in those hours he was not thinking like himself; he was only reacting, trying to hold himself together so he would not collapse in front of her.

Afterwards, he finds that the event does not stay in the past. It comes back in flashes when he least expects it: while trying to fall asleep, standing in the kitchen, or hearing a sudden noise that pulls him right back into the panic of that day. He says the images arrive without permission, sharp and physical, like his body knows the memory before his mind does. He will sometimes freeze for a moment, stare at nothing, and then realize he has missed part of a conversation. He does not like driving near the place where it happened, and if he has to pass that area, his chest tightens and his hands grip the wheel so hard that his knuckles ache. He avoids talking about the accident with people outside the house, partly because he does not want their pity and partly because words seem to make the memory more real.

His wife is home with him now, and their marriage has become both a comfort and a source of strain. He is protective in a way that sometimes surprises even him. He checks on her repeatedly, watches for signs that something bad is about to happen, and reads into small changes in her tone or movement. If she is late answering a text, he imagines the worst. He knows this makes him seem tense and controlling, but he says he cannot stop scanning for danger. He has become jumpy around sudden sounds, especially car alarms, dropped objects, or a phone ringing unexpectedly. His sleep is broken by vivid dreams, and he wakes disoriented, his heart racing before he is fully aware of where he is. Some nights he stays awake longer than he should, not because he wants to, but because sleep feels like a place where he has less control over what his mind will show him.

Since the trauma, he notices himself pulling away from people. He is polite with family and friends, but he is less open than he used to be. He can sit in a room and feel far away from everyone in it. He worries that others expect him to "be strong," and he feels ashamed when he cannot manage that. He says he used to imagine himself as someone practical and calm, someone who would get a job, take care of his wife, and move forward. Now he often feels older than 21 and younger at the same time, as if the event interrupted his life before it had really started. Even on better days, there is a sense that he is waiting for the next blow. He goes through the motions of looking for work, helping around the house, and being present for his wife, but underneath it all he remains braced, as if his body has not yet gotten the message that the emergency has passed.
